title: Square Enix accidentally botches a Nier: Automata update, balloons required file size from 50GB to 366GB on PC, but don't worry, there's a fix
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
"Do you think games are silly little things?"

Yesterday, Nier: Automata received a new patch on Steam, adding more language support to the title - it can now be played with Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese options - but this new update also, somehow, inflated the file size of the game on PC from about 50GB to 366GB. D'oh! What's worse is, the update is not optional.

The cause of this, reportedly, is a bug that caused all the DLC in the YoRHa Edition of the game to become the same size as the base game - and the new download stacks them all concurrently. "Only SquareEnix can turn 40GB into 366GB with 8GB patch," says one dissatisfied Steam reviewer.

If you don't have space for this massive new file on your PC (and I can't say I blame you, it's ridiculous), there is a workaround, as confirmed by Square Enix in a tweet via its Japanese Twitter account.

"We have confirmed an issue where, following the latest update to the Steam version of Nier: Automata, the installation process indicates that more storage space is required than expected," noted the publisher. "We are currently investigating the cause and working on a solution. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. As a temporary workaround, you can download the base game by unchecking the DLC under Steam → Properties → DLC."

It's quite ironic, really, that so many Steam reviewers are complaining about things like "I just need to delete 90% of my computer to install this" when a large part of the game is managing the software/programmes installed on your android protagonists in order to upgrade your abilities and stats. There's even an ending for uninstalling your OS on your mechanical main characters. I'd be inclined to suggest this is some sort of meta psy-op from creator Yoko Taro, but… nah, that's just fantasy, isn't it? Isn't it?

Speaking of Taro, earlier this year we learned that "Nier Automata will continue", though we only heard back in 2025 that most of the projects the developer was working on were cancelled. One of these may have been the Tencent-backed Nier mobile game in 2024, which reportedly "struggled to find a monetisation to offset its high costs."

title: Humble Bundle redesign removes two-factor verification from settings
author: Jay Peters
content:
Jay Peters

is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The Humble Bundle storefront for buying games and other software recently got a new look, but on the settings page, it no longer offers a way to add or update two-factor verification methods, as reported by Kotaku. PC Gamer also points out that there are Humble Bundle support pages discussing two-factor verification, and the writer for the publication said that they had set up two-factor verification on the old version of the site.

However, it does appear that, at least as of now, there is some form of two-factor verification. When I tried logging into my Humble Bundle account while writing this article, I was prompted to check my email for an access code before I could access my account. While logged in, I was able to update my password, but I didn’t have to enter my old password to be able to do so.

For what it’s worth, my passwords app also shows that I set up a rotating two-factor code for Humble Bundle at some point. I was not asked to input that at any part of my login process today.

Humble Bundle owner IGN Entertainment and IGN parent company Ziff Davis didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

title: My 99-Year-Old Grandmother Built a Hidden Empire Around Flannel. Then She Lost It All.
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
For Outside, Yoon Kim recounts how his Korean grandmother helped pioneer the industrial production of cotton flannel in postwar Seoul. It’s a moving family history, as well as a pointed look at today’s outdoor industry, which is still very white, particularly in leadership roles.

Sonia, now 31 years old, blossomed as a business owner and entrepreneur. Most of Baeekyang Gimo’s customers were wholesalers and garment manufacturers throughout Korea. Sonia took orders from small businesses in Seoul’s Pyeonghwa Market in the Dongdaemun district and sold large orders to garment factories in Daegu. Even the Korean military was using their flannel in standard-issue uniforms. Baeekyang Gimo was profitable in its first year. By the societal standards of the time, Sonia’s work was almost unheard of. Women in postwar Korea worked hard, but they toiled in the background: in fields, markets, or family shops where a husband or father was the face and the owner. Confucian tradition places a woman at the bottom of a social pyramid: under her father, her husband, and even her son, for life.

title: Southern Democrats Repudiate MAGA Racism
author: @NewYorker
content:
Since the 2024 Presidential race, Donald Trump has wrapped himself in the argument that white people are the real victims of racism. This January, in the lead-up to Martin Luther King, Jr., Day, Trump went even further, claiming that the protections initiated in the sixties under the Civil Rights Act led to white people being treated “very badly.” Trump’s acolytes have parroted his claims of white victimhood as an explanation for downward mobility and hardship. Vice-President J. D. Vance has repeatedly claimed that white men, in particular, are victims of racial discrimination. In the closing crescendo of the midterm campaign, much of his venom was directed at Michigan’s Democratic candidate for senator, Abdul El-Sayed, who, Vance said, had “hatred in his heart” for the state’s people and places. “Perhaps,” Vance added, “it’s because he sees them as too white or too proud or too American.”

Apparently, there is an expiration date on the red-meat racism of Trumpism. El-Sayed defeated his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, by seven points. Elsewhere, Republicans attempted to link Black candidates to chaos and crime, but these tried-and-true tactics appear to have had little effect. Angie Nixon, a Florida state representative and union organizer, ran an upstart campaign for the U.S. Senate, and was subject to witheringly racist attacks from the President and his supporters. Laura Loomer, who boasts of her access to Trump, described Nixon as “a ghetto, black, communist.” She mocked Nixon’s speech as “Ebonics” and wrote, “Maybe I need to bark at you and tug your leash and then you’ll finally understand.” Trump said of Nixon, “She’s not of the intellect that should be running for the Senate. She’s a very-low-I.Q. person.” Yet Nixon—who ran a campaign centered on Medicare for All, universal child care, and taxing billionaires—came within three points of defeating the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, converting an estimated six per cent of Floridians who voted for Trump in 2024.

In the Georgia gubernatorial race, the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, was pitted against the Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire health-care executive who spent more than two hundred million dollars of his own money on the election. Bottoms, who served as the mayor of Atlanta during Trump’s first term, gained prominence during those years as one of the President’s opponents: she denied ICE the right to hold detainees in the city’s jail, in response to the Administration’s family-detention practices, and opposed the rapid reopening of Georgia at the height of the pandemic. Jackson, a white man, repeatedly blamed Bottoms for violent crime in Atlanta and for the 2020 unrest in response to police brutality—often conflating the two. Not to be outdone, Trump held a rally outside of Macon, where he accused Bottoms of having “destroyed Atlanta with her crime and filth and constant riots.” She won the race by nearly nine percentage points, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of any state. Across Georgia, seven other Black women won statewide seats.

In Louisiana, Jamie Davis, a third-generation Black farmer, ran for the Senate on what he called the “four pillars” of affordability, education, health care, and upholding the Constitution. He also supported a moratorium on building new data centers and pledged to introduce legislation barring elected officials from signing nondisclosure agreements. According to a local news investigation, his opponent, Representative Julia Letlow, signed an N.D.A. with Meta about a fifty-billion-dollar data-center project in her district; she went on to purchase stock in Meta and then failed to disclose those trades for more than a year, in violation of federal law. (In response to the reporting, a spokesperson for Letlow said that these purchases were made by a broker and that she did not direct any of her trades.)

Astonishingly, Davis was neck and neck with Letlow well into the fall, when, in an act of desperation, a Republican PAC released an ad showing an A.I.-generated Davis lumbering toward the camera in a T-shirt and jeans. A Louisiana Republican pollster, Bernie Pinsonat, explained to a local Fox News affiliate that the ad was intended “to turn any whites off that would think about voting for him. You know, we do have a lot of RINOs”—Republicans in Name Only—“in this state.” Davis came within two points of Letlow, losing by a mere twenty-five thousand votes. The Fox News Voter Poll for Louisiana estimates that he earned the support of ninety-two per cent of Black voters, thirty-four per cent of white voters, and eleven per cent of people who said they had voted for Trump in 2024. Every parish shifted toward Democrats by at least nine points.

The outcome may well have been different had Davis received meaningful assistance from the national Democratic Party. Days before the election, the longtime Democratic Party consultant and Louisiana native son James Carville noted, “I beat my head against the wall trying to get some national money in here. It’s almost impossible.” Scott Colom, the Democratic Senate candidate in Mississippi, whose exceedingly close race was called in his favor on Wednesday, was also left out in the cold. In July, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee made a forty-million-dollar investment in ten Senate battlegrounds, part of which funded outreach to Black voters, that did not include Mississippi—even though a poll had shown that Colom was within three points of the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. Finally, the D.S.C.C. joined Colom on a five-hundred-thousand-dollar ad buy with just six days left to vote.

Even near-misses, such as Jamie Davis’s and Angie Nixon’s Senate bids, convey a larger truth about the midterm elections. Two years after Trump’s return, his appeals to white supremacy and victimhood can’t compensate for voters’ struggles with the cost-of-living crisis, disgust with Trump’s corruption, or rage at the billionaires’ prerogative to put data centers anywhere they please. In races across the South, Democratic candidates attracted the support of a wide swath of voters. Their campaigns are evidence of the viability of class politics in every corner of the country. In Mississippi, a remarkable nine per cent of residents who voted for Trump in 2024 voted for Colom in 2026. In Louisiana, one field organizer for Davis said, “I’ve never worked with Republicans this much. Ever.”

The G.O.P.’s racist attacks may not have worked to turn out white voters, but they undoubtedly helped to mobilize Black voters. These date back to the Administration’s war on D.E.I.—specifically, its attack on Black workers in the federal government, led by Elon Musk and the short-lived DOGE. By September, 2026, federal employment had fallen by roughly three hundred and twenty-eight thousand jobs since Trump took office. Multiple lawsuits have alleged that the firings targeted Black workers, who made up roughly eighteen per cent of the federal workforce in 2024. (The Trump Administration has responded that its firings were not racially biased.) The attacks on Black employment were amplified by the continued evisceration of the Voting Rights Act. After the Supreme Court’s Callais decision, in April—which allowed states to redraw, or “crack,” districts that concentrated Black voters to assure their representation—Louisiana dismantled its second majority-Black congressional district, Tennessee split Memphis’s Black communities among three districts, and Alabama reinstated a map that reduced Black voters’ share of the voting-age population in its Second Congressional District.

Just two years ago, Republicans boasted about their new currency with Black men and Latino voters. But the A.P. Voter Poll estimates that, this year, about ninety per cent of Black voters supported Democratic House candidates; roughly eighty per cent backed Kamala Harris in 2024. Only about ten per cent of Black male voters supported Republican candidates, just two years after approximately twenty-five per cent cast ballots for Trump. In Louisiana, where the Callais case originated, Black voters cast more than eighty-six thousand early and absentee ballots—an eighty-three-per-cent increase from the 2022 midterms.

In Alabama, Representative Shomari Figures, a Democrat, won reëlection in the cracked Second Congressional District by nearly eight points. The candidates in Louisiana’s cracked Sixth District are headed to a runoff election. In Tennessee, the Democratic state representative Justin J. Pearson ran in a newly configured district, which previously was centered on Memphis and now stretches over roughly two hundred miles, only to lose by some twenty-five hundred votes to his Republican opponent. In fourteen of the fifteen counties making up the new seat, Republican majorities voted for Trump in the 2024 election. Across these counties, Pearson won 48.5 per cent of the vote.

Pearson is a longtime progressive activist, but not all of these candidates are on the left—Davis ran as a gun-toting farmer and business owner. Nearly all of them, however, campaigned on the affordability crisis, which extends far beyond the cost of gas. Their campaigns upend the assumption of many Democratic consultants that rural and Southern outposts are a poor use of financial resources and political talent. Whether they mark a political turning point will depend upon whether Democrats now choose to take the whole of America, and especially the South, seriously. If Party leaders invest in the Southern candidates who are attracting Black, white, and brown voters and rebuilding regional political organizations, they may find the source of a sustained electoral turnaround. If they do not, we can expect right-wing forces to reassemble a possibly more dangerous version of Trumpism—more serious, more determined, and more destructive. ♦

title: Skyrim lead designer hopes Sentinel will finally solve The Elder Scrolls' ladder problem
author: Sherif Saed
content:
"It seems simple, it seems stupid."

For such a simple, straightforward real-world object, ladders have been the bane of game developers' existence since the early days of the industry. And Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls Series is certainly no stranger to that struggle.

While we may be years away from the release of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, the recent title reveal reignited conversations about what longtime fans hope to see from it. That includes former Bethesda developers, such as Skyrim lead designer and Bethesda veteran Bruce Nesmith, who picked ladders as one thing he hopes Sentinel actually figures out.

If you're unfamiliar, ladders in Skyrim work in a weird way. You don't animatedly climb up and down them, but rather the character simply teleports from one end to the other. Speaking to The Examined Game (via GamesRadar+), Nesmith said that Skyrim's approach "really limits the art team in terms of how you can do multi-layer [levels]".

"It seems simple, it seems stupid, but you don't climb up and down ladders," said Nesmith. "All the ladders in Skyrim, you click on the ladder, poof, you're at the top or you have to climb a stair.

"But to do ladders, you have to deal with a whole host of questions which our programmers very legitimately put in front of us and said, 'You give me answers to these, I'll tell you how much programming time it's going to take to make them.' And you know, that caused problems right there."

Nesmith then pointed out the hidden complexity of creating functioning ladders in games, and the scenarios developers have to anticipate and account for, especially in a game as dynamic as an Elder Scrolls title.

"So, I'm halfway up a ladder, and [an] NPC decides to climb down it. What happens?" Nesmith posited. "The NPC has to have AI that will adjust for that. Does the player go through the NPC? Is he blocked by the NPC? Does the NPC stay on the ladder? Does the NPC go back up and know to wait and then come back down?

"And I'm just scratching the surface of some of the problems they brought up. So, it seems simple, and other games have climbing ladders, but we chose to put our efforts into other things to make them better rather than deal with that. So, I'd like to see Bethesda finally come around to making ladders a reality where you're actually climbing them and make the world feel a little more immersive."

While we know very little about Sentinel right now - much less how it's going to solve the ladder problem -that hasn't stopped fans from speculating about a number of topics, including what they believe is going to be a split / alternate timeline setup.

title: PlayStation delays God of War Laufey by three months, as Sony Santa Monica escapes a packed February and moves its PS5 exclusive to May
author: Kaan Serin
content:
"We will make the most of each moment until then."

God of War Laufey has been delayed. Sony Santa Monica's PS5 exclusive is now dodging the crowded month of February and will instead come out on 20th May, 2027.

Developer Sony Santa Monica announced it's pushing back the upcoming action epic via a brief social media post. While the studio stopped short of giving a reason for the delay, it did say it's using the extra time to polish Faye's solo adventure.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen. We don't take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans," the studio wrote.

"With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20th, 2027," the statement continued. "We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey is notably the first game in the famed PlayStation series to not star Kratos in the lead role. This time around, Faye takes the lead through a version of the afterlife that houses gods and deities from multiple mythologies - and it's bringing back the original series' faster combat, too.

Of course, Kratos will return in future God of War games (he also shows up here and there during Faye's romp), and whatever that next Kratos game becomes, it'll supposedly connect to the events of Laufey, according to the developer.

On the bright side, the delay might be good news for anyone worried about their impossibly large and ever expanding backlogs. February 2027 is already packed with really exciting games - from the Fable reboot and Persona 4 Revival to Metro 2039. Hopefully, Laufey's delay gives everyone more breathing room.

title: Sick BMX flips, colourful characters, a whole lot of mail and a charming raccoon dog await you in Tanuki: Pon's Summer, which you can pick up now
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Something to warm you up this winter

Right, today's been miserable thanks to the now hourly discourse we have to all take part in lest we be seen as approving of the current bad thing, how about something that looks simply pleasant? Today's the launch day for Tanuki: Pon's Summer, a delightfully vibrant mail delivery sim/Tony Hawk's Pro Skater but for bikes about restoring a shrine before the end of summer.

I've been enamoured by the vibe of Tanuki: Pon's Summer since it was announced in no small part because of how in some small ways it reminds me of Boku No Natsuyasumi, a cult-classic, Japan-only game series that's mostly just about hanging out in the Japanese countryside. This one isn't so lackadaisical, as you do have a job to do in delivering mail, but I think a similar spirit is there.

When it comes to delivering mail, there is a Death Strandingian element to it in your need to place your boxes on your BMX (which you can do sick tricks and flips on, of course) to maximise how much you can deliver. A bit less stressful than Kojima's joint, obviously, though elements are still there. Any money you earn from this gig can then be spent on restoring the shrine that you oh so love, which falls onto the sim side of things with the ability to fully customise how the shrine looks.

There are also a whole heap of minigames to perform that helps you get to know the locals. I'm talking baseball, sumo wrestling, working in a sushi restaurant and, of course, fishing. You can see bits of that in the launch trailer above, which comes with as 2010s an anime opening song you could wish for with some animation so good it makes me want an adaptation of the game. In time, perhaps! You can pick it up on Steam right here.

title: I Am a 2026 National Book Award Finalist. The U.S. Denied My Visa
author: @NewYorker
content:
When the U.S. consular officer grinned and offered her hearty congratulations on my award nomination, I almost believed my visa interview might turn out differently than I’d anticipated.

“Such a huge accomplishment!” she said, beaming.

I’d been preparing for the interview for weeks, rehearsing my answers to every question I could imagine. My hand rested on a stack of transparent dossiers, each color-coded for quick access. One, marked with a yellow label, held my statement of purpose, explaining that my memoir, “Huna,” was a finalist for the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction and that I was expected to attend the finalist reading and award ceremony in New York in mid-November. Behind it, another dossier with an orange label contained my publisher’s invitation letter, my confirmed itinerary, and a sheet of contact information for the publisher and the National Book Foundation.

If I was asked about my history of political incarceration, I would reach for blue: the prison folder. It contained court documents, a case file from a Geneva-based human-rights organization, and a 2023 New York Times article about my six years as a political prisoner in post-revolution Egypt, the subject of my memoir. I was prepared to explain how I had been jailed as a teen-ager for protesting the 2013 military coup, given a fifteen-year sentence, and released in 2020, after one of my family’s many appeals was arbitrarily reviewed, exposing that I had been wrongfully tried as an adult instead of as a minor.

To answer questions about my ties outside the U.S., I would reach for green. That dossier held my current European residence permit, a one-year apartment lease, and confirmed U.K. and European book-tour events for the year ahead—evidence that I would leave the U.S. once my brief visit was over. I had a few more thematic dossiers, plus a final, unlabelled one for miscellaneous documents, just in case. Through it all, one anxious thought swirled in my head: Please don’t ask me about politics. Please don’t ask me why I left the U.S.

When my turn came, I stepped up to the window and deployed a persona that I’d refined over countless visa interviews and “chats” with border-control officers: open posture, steady eye contact, an easy smile with just the right amount of earnestness. I had to be prepared enough to show I had a legitimate reason to visit and enough funds, but not so prepared, so eager, that I came across as someone with something to hide. Desperate people, after all, are the ones who overstay their visas or, God forbid, immigrate. The trick was to exude the nonchalance of having nothing to prove while making absolutely sure that I proved everything.

The interview began more smoothly than I’d expected. One by one, the suspicions attached to my passport seemed to fall away. The consular officer nodded at the Penguin Random House letterhead, the printout of the National Book Foundation web page; appeared reassured that my flights and accommodation were fully covered; squinted and nodded at my European residence permit. Even my political incarceration took up less space in the conversation than I’d feared. The tension in her eyes seemed to ease as she saw the Times logo and profile.

I exhaled.

She typed a few words into her computer, then scrolled down her screen. Her expression tightened.

“Unfortunately, I can’t decide on this application now. We have to consult Washington first, then get back to you.”

My stomach dropped. She told me that I’d be placed in administrative processing and that the decision would be e-mailed once she heard back from Washington. I thanked her and went home. The next morning, I woke to a formal visa denial in my inbox. They wouldn’t put in writing what the system had flagged or the reason that Washington provided overnight, only that I was found ineligible for a visitor visa under the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Years ago, in my prison cell in Egypt, I used to fantasize about writing a memoir. I would slip under a bright red duvet my mother had bribed the guards to let through, and imagine that everything happening to me would end up in a book. That a guard’s baton was battering not my ribs but those of the book’s protagonist. That a slap was landing on the protagonist’s face, not mine. I was the author, concerned only with how I would render the torture my body was undergoing on the page.

For six years and three months, I wrote steadily, smuggling the pages out one visit at a time. I started reading contraband books with an eye for craft, trying to reverse engineer the lines that lingered and emulate their moves. The scribbles on a smuggled page became a potential essay, the essay a potential published article, the article a book. I would imagine it winning an award. Hours passed as I delivered fictional acceptance speeches under Mama’s duvet, revising and honing them, fleetingly unincarcerated. Prison was my horizon, but this fantasy, despite the unhealthy dissociation from my body it entailed, helped. And in prison, if something helps, you keep doing it.

After my release, I kept writing, publishing essays and political commentary about my experience and that of politically incarcerated friends, many of whom are still behind bars. Before long, well-connected relatives warned me that my name was circulating as a potential target for rearrest. I fled Egypt that same year and began working on my book while moving constantly between countries in search of the next visa, for a semblance of home. Then, in 2022, I received a full ride to pursue an M.F.A. in nonfiction writing at the University of Pittsburgh.

The three years I spent at Pitt were crucial to the creation of my book. I made a home, found my people, and built a warm, tender literary community, one I lean on to this day. The M.F.A. also offered more tangible assistance: access to legal status, funds, mobility, access. I applied for swaths of research and travel grants, attended every literary conference I could, spoke on every stage, and put myself and my developing book in every room. I was building a life, but I was also stocking the color-coded dossiers I carried everywhere, assembling evidence that I was extraordinary enough to be allowed to keep that life.

In 2023, I found a literary agent and worked more intensely toward a full manuscript. I was disheartened to learn that only U.S. citizens could submit to major literary awards such as the Pulitzer and the National Book Awards. But, following years of advocacy by the organization Undocupoets and by writers such as the Salvadoran poet Javier Zamora, the Pulitzer Prize Board announced, in 2023, that it would expand the eligibility criteria for some categories, opening the award to authors with permanent residence, or whose primary, long-term home was in the United States. The National Book Foundation followed suit in 2024. The fantasy that had sustained me under my mother’s prison duvet for years was suddenly within reach.

Meanwhile, I worried about what would happen once my student visa expired. When the offer for “Huna” from Hogarth, an imprint of Penguin Random House, landed in my inbox in 2024, my agent called. Her first words were a thrilled “Congratulations”; my first words, breathless: “Can they write me a letter for an O-1 extraordinary-ability visa?”

After Trump returned to power in 2025, ICE was unleashed against immigrant communities and pro-Palestine international students. In the aftermath of October 7th, I had attended rallies on campus and written political commentary for outlets such as Foreign Policy and the Washington Post. I had criticized the relationship between Egypt and the U.S., and argued that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza—a position I believe should never have needed to be defended—and that this must fundamentally alter our understanding of international law. I knew that my activism put me at risk of being arrested.

My sense of risk escalated as I watched Rümeysa Öztürk, a Turkish national and Tufts Ph.D. student, get snatched off the street by ICE agents near her home, for co-authoring an op-ed relating to Gaza. I consulted lawyers who warned me that, given my public profile, my arrest was likely a matter of time. Concerned as I was about ICE detention, deportation to Egypt carried an even more terrifying prospect: imprisonment for the rest of my life.

I spent the month of April, 2025, revising my book behind the locked door of my apartment. I deactivated some of my social-media accounts and made others private. I cancelled readings and speaking engagements. My friends Kira, Miles, and laura scanned the street around my apartment every day, trying to make sure it was clear of undercover ICE agents before sneaking me into their cars like contraband. One day, I caught myself wondering what I wanted to be wearing when ICE came to my door. At that moment, I recognized the logic of the system that I had fled to the U.S. to escape—one in which speaking and writing openly made you a target and the possibility of imprisonment reorganized the smallest routines of daily life.

I knew then that I had to uproot my life again. I left the U.S. in late April and resettled in Europe, entering what I hoped would be a temporary exile within my exile. I attended my M.F.A. graduation remotely, and lost the chance to tour the country for my book, to celebrate with the people who had become my people.

When I learned that “Huna” had been long-listed for the National Book Award, and, weeks later, received a call from a 212 number telling me I was a finalist for the award, my joy was tempered by the fact that I could not share the experience with the friends who had witnessed the book’s journey. This visitor-visa application was my last stab at a homecoming—if only for a few days.

Visas, awards, travel: these are the problems of an unincarcerated person. As a seventeen-year-old boy shrinking in the corner of a cell, I fantasized about a day when these would be my problems. Back then, a life beyond prison, where my dreams could be crushed in this way, was itself the dream. This is why I write about those I left behind: Ayman, whose brown eyes creased as he joked torture away in our cell; Tooha, whose gap-toothed smile shone as he held me in Wadi Al-Natroun prison after our appeal was rejected; Adel, whose laugh buoyed me as we shouted through the peepholes in our cell doors, keeping each other company through the night. I dream that they, too, might be afforded a life in which stacking their color-coded dossiers is their most pressing concern. Still, there is a particular cruelty to being forced to outrun the fruits of one’s labor, to watch one’s work bloom from afar. My book has made it into rooms that I never will. I don’t know what to do with that, and so I write. ♦

title: You May be Able to Get 43 More Minutes of Work Done if You Change Your Desk - Nautilus
content:
Have you ever wished you had an extra hour in the day? Well, if you’ll settle for roughly 45 minutes, I’ve got good news for you. A new study published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics found that workers can squeeze 43 minutes of extra productivity out of their day, just by using a sit-stand desk. 

A team of occupational and public health researchers from Texas A&M University discovered the productivity benefits of these adjustable-height desks, which exploded in popularity around the time sitting was declared “the new smoking,” after studying more than 10,000 workers who worked at a large California energy company. They surveyed the workers about their comfort and tracked their computer activity digitally, capturing everything from keystrokes and mouse clicks to words typed and typos.

Read more: “Your Boss Is Watching You”

They found that workers who used the height-adjustable desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time per day, compared with just 2.95 hours among those using old-fashioned sit-only desks. Over a year, that adds up to roughly 170 hours of work or four 40-hour workweeks. The sit-standers also made more keystrokes and typed more words (although this speedy typing resulted in slightly more typos). Both groups were equally comfortable (or uncomfortable).  

The productivity gains could add up to big bucks, too. According to their back-of-the-envelope calculations using a $52 per hour wage, sit-stand desks may be able to generate roughly $9,000 in annual productivity value per employee (this is where your boss’s eyes turn into dollar signs). 

“Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” study author Mark Benden said in a statement. “The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way.”

There’s one caveat, however: This wasn’t a randomized controlled trial. Instead of being randomly assigned workstations, employees were allowed to choose whether they wanted a sitting or standing desk as part of a company wellness program. It’s possible that the more conscientious workers simply opted for adjustable desks. 

Still, there are countless studies on the health risks posed by living a sedentary life, so if you don’t want a height-adjustable desk for your productivity, consider one for your health.

title: Joe Biden’s New Memoir Shows a Man in Denial
author: @NewYorker
content:
The last time Joe Biden published a memoir, called “Promise Me, Dad,” nine years ago, he ended up getting his ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, in a certain amount of trouble. Zwonitzer had recorded interviews he conducted with Biden, including one in February, 2017, at Biden’s rental home in Virginia, in which the then former Vice-President told him, “I just found all the classified stuff downstairs!” That recording would eventually become public because more classified stuff would later be found at a University of Pennsylvania office that Biden used, and then still more at his Delaware home, leading to the appointment of a special counsel, Robert Hur, in 2023. Zwonitzer was subpoenaed, had his computer taken, faced the prospect of criminal charges, and was referred by House Republicans for contempt of Congress. Years of litigation ensued.

Zwonitzer, who also worked with Biden on a 2007 memoir, “Promises to Keep,” is not mentioned in the former President’s latest offering, “Promise Me, America,” which is out next week. (Judging from the acknowledgments, Biden relied on a number of people this time, among them Ted Widmer, a historian whose recent work includes a volume on the Declaration of Independence and an oral history of the band Wings.) Biden gives an account of the classified-documents investigation that focusses, instead, on his rage at Hur, who wrote, in his final report on the case, that the President came across, in his interview with the special counsel, as a “sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory.” Biden calls this “extraneous commentary” and a “gratuitous hit.” It was neither. Biden’s forgetfulness was a reason that Hur cited for not prosecuting the President: if a jury believed that Biden had honestly forgotten about the classified documents, it would have been hard to get a conviction.

By any reckoning, the question of Biden’s general competency during his Presidency is a crucial one; doubts about his fitness ended his campaign for reëlection, after all. But “Promise Me, America” treats all such inquiries as extraneous and gratuitous, not just Hur’s. Biden allows that his June, 2024, debate with Donald Trump (who had his own issues with classified documents) had “gone badly” but adds that “debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent Presidents.” He sees no qualitative distinction between his frightening and heartbreaking lack of focus that night and Barack Obama’s subpar performance against Mitt Romney, or George W. Bush being “caught with a scowling face” in his debate with John Kerry: “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate.” Biden continues to find it unfair that he was not afforded that opportunity. He blames “the narrative” and disloyal Democrats for the fact that he had to drop out, which he did three and a half weeks after the debate. “I wasn’t living in a dream world,” he writes. “I believed I was the best person to lead the world.”

Incredibly, Biden sticks to that position, even though, in May, 2025, when his second term would have barely been under way, he announced that he had been diagnosed with Stage IV prostate cancer. The disease had metastasized to his bones and, based on what is known as its Gleason score of nine, was fast-moving. His doctors, it emerged, had stuck to the general practice of not routinely screening men older than seventy. (Biden turned eighty in 2022.) In his memoir, Biden answers the question of whether this was wise when the patient was the Commander-in-Chief with a resounding “maybe.” He adds that he was surprised that people were “cynical” enough to think that he might not have been honest about his health. (In February, 2024, three weeks after the Hur report, that same medical team declared him “healthy, active, robust” and “fit for duty.”) It took an interview with People magazine this week to wrest from him the concession that, had he known he had advanced cancer, he wouldn’t have run. “But that wasn’t the case,” he said, still insisting that on “an objective basis” he was the right man for the job. The People interview has been his only one tied to the release of the memoir; in an X post, he said that there wouldn’t be a traditional press tour because the cancer treatment sometimes “slows me down.”

The news of the memoir, in short, is that there is no real news: Biden is as stubbornly in denial as ever. And that assessment risks making the book sound more interesting than it is. Apart from the few, frustrating stretches on his reëlection decision (from which one would never know that he had once referred to himself as “a bridge,” a phrase widely understood to mean that he would serve only a single term), most of “Promise Me, America” is startlingly dull. Much of it has the feel of something written by a committee—and a committee of which Biden himself need not have been a member. Even the headline-making detail, from an early excerpt, in The Atlantic, that on entering the White House in January, 2021, Biden found a note from Trump that was more friendly and circumspect than one would expect from a man who had been trying to overturn the election—“I know how much you love the American people”—is of marginal interest, and really about Trump, not Biden. The advance Biden received for the book was reportedly about ten million dollars.

There are whole pages that read as if someone simply sat down with Biden’s public schedule and speeches and patched them together with a few judicious additions of the first person (“As I said in my welcoming remarks . . .”) and references to America’s past (Lincoln, the gold rush, D Day). A description of a meeting in the Situation Room includes the names and job titles of a dozen people, followed by nothing much illuminating about how they may have interacted or clashed, or about how power in the White House actually worked. Some attendance lists are compelling in themselves, such as the log of phone calls that Biden made in the hours after he dropped out. (Bill Clinton is on it; Obama is not.) But when intimate details about encounters with senators or world leaders do appear, they too often have footnotes that lead to contemporary press coverage or public statements. The source listed for Angela Merkel’s blunt criticism of Trump, for example, is a Guardian article about her memoir. Instead of any real introspection, we get cliché. After a mention of threats posed by China and Russia: “Given these choppy waters, I was glad to be steering the ship of state.”

One of the themes of Biden’s memoir is that he was a fantastic President. To hear him tell it, as his term was coming to an end, things were going great all around. The global economy was “humming,” inflation in the U.S. was falling, we’d “completely rebuilt NATO” and “reclaimed the American advantage over China,” carbon emissions were poised to plunge, and the A.I. companies had meekly fallen in line with his call for them to be more responsible actors. And there were real successes. It would be a far better book if he acknowledged some failure other than not retaining the loyalty of Democratic leaders.

For example, as part of his claim to have beaten COVID, he writes that it took him just four months, until May, 2021, to go “from fewer than half of America’s schools being open to 99 percent.” If that number is news to many parents, it is because Biden seems to be defining “open” as a school where a child showed up at some point, rather than consistently or full time, and ignoring reclosures in the wake of the Omicron variant. (An earlier book, Franklin Foer’s “The Last Politician,” explored the role Joe Biden’s relationship with teachers’ unions played in the struggle to reopen schools, for better or worse.)

There is similar sleight of hand in his discussion of immigration. Biden boasts of a dramatic fall in “encounters with undocumented migrants” at the border between January, 2021, and January, 2025. At the same time, the Biden years did see a historic wave of immigration, and the memoir offers little insight into how it was managed. For example, he does not mention his Administration’s concurrent extension or renewal of Temporary Protected Status to more than a million people, and of humanitarian parole to hundreds of thousands more, many of whom were fleeing terrible circumstances. Those migrants were documented, but, because T.P.S. grants and parole are executive-branch actions, Biden also left them vulnerable to having their status stripped away by the next Administration—which it promptly began doing, as Trump turned migrants into targets.

“Yes, people could point to moments when I mixed up names or lost my train of thought or had a weak voice or walked slowly,” Biden writes. “But they could never point to something presidential that I failed to do.” A few pages later, he points to one. It is the spring of 2024, several months after Hamas brutally murdered civilians in Israel, including at a music festival, taking many of the survivors hostage, and Biden has repeatedly spoken to Benjamin Netanyahu to express his “concerns” about the Israeli military response, and what “rising casualties were doing to Israel’s image.” To his dismay, he writes, “Bibi had no qualms about making promises he had no power—or intention—to keep.” Be that as it may, it also appears that the promises Netanyahu made—to act with restraint, to protect civilians—were ones that Biden no longer had the strength or resolve to enforce. The combination of an ever-mendacious Netanyahu and an increasingly diminished Biden was a disastrous one. In many situations, a good team of staff members can act on behalf of a President, but there are moments when a President is required to impose his or her will, as only a President can. That moment came for Biden after October 7th, and he missed it.

Biden’s wife, Jill Biden, published her own memoir earlier this year. To read them side by side is to be reminded that there is more than one way of being avoidant. Jill padded her book with details about the White House’s floral arrangements; Joe does so with a six-page list of laws he signed, including the CHIPS and Science Act and the Working Dog Health and Welfare Act. The Biden Administration did accomplish a great deal—the legislation passed, the trillions of dollars spent—but it could be notably lacking in transparency, and the President’s memoir doesn’t much help. He speaks more kindly of his Vice-President, Kamala Harris, than Jill does, for example, but without giving a real sense of her influence or why he thought that she would be ready to step in for him, either when he chose her as his running mate or when he endorsed her, twenty-seven minutes after he withdrew from the race.

Where the Jill and Joe memoirs converge is in their repeated, deeply felt invocations of Biden’s older son, Beau, who died of brain cancer in 2015. (Both Bidens also view the younger, troubled Biden son, Hunter, as a martyr-like target of partisan attacks; neither expresses regret for Joe’s decision to grant him, along with other relatives and allies, a broad pardon before leaving office.) Beau’s appearances are the most Bidenesque part of “Promise Me, America,” and the places where Biden’s own mark is most clear. The promise in “Promise Me, Dad,” the 2017 memoir, was Beau’s request that Joe not be so undone by his death that he withdrew from politics.

Beau is also part of Biden’s explanation for his enduring anger at Robert Hur, who said in his report that Biden didn’t know what year it was that Beau died. In his memoir, Biden calls this claim “outrageous,” adding, “if Robert Hur wants to know when my son died, here’s my answer: Today. I wake up every day feeling like I just lost him a minute ago.” But the transcript of their interview shows that Hur was correct. The Hur report matters because, in retrospect, it offered Democrats an opening to replace Biden on the ticket, at a time when only four states had held primaries, and Super Tuesday was still a month away, making it less likely that a decent President would be replaced by an awful one. But it matters in assessing Biden’s memoir, too.

Throughout his career, Biden’s signature rhetorical subject has been how a person pushes on in the face of grief and mourning. As a young man, he lost his first wife and his baby daughter in a car crash. He had it in him to write a great book about the loss of his own powers as he aged, and how it led him to lash out at people like Hur, who said what they saw, and at allies who loved him but knew that he was done. He might have found a way to be grateful for a debate that, aberration or not, insured that he wouldn’t take the oath of office with an undiagnosed case of cancer, and regretful that he didn’t depart the stage even sooner. That this memoir is not that book is a literary as well as a political tragedy. The one thing Biden doesn’t know how to mourn, it seems, is his Presidency. ♦
